title: global markets breakingviews 2026 08 29
author: Liam Proud
text:
LONDON, Aug 29 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Welcome back! Liam here, filling in for Peter Thal Larsen. Anthropic’s initial public offering seems close. As you read the listing document, keep in mind some lessons from my colleague Karen Kwok’s coverage. To summarise: the Claude developer’s recent growth deceleration is no cause for panic; its shares could serve as M&A currency; the risks include corporate AI fatigue, governments and open-source models; and “run-rate” revenue figures are misleading. More ​to add? Email me
, opens new tab
. (If this newsletter was forwarded to you, sign up here to get it in your inbox every weekend.)
“How do you know when a hedge fund manager is talking his book? His ‌mouth is moving.”
Read more: Beware hedge fund managers trashing US policy.
No CEO wants to be in the position that Mark Zuckerberg found himself in this week. His tech giant Meta Platforms (META.O)
, opens new tab
 on Wednesday agreed to pay up to $18 ​billion to settle claims, made by nearly all U.S. states, that the company designed Facebook and Instagram to keep children addicted to social media.
Still, its shares ended the day ⁠up 1%, indicating either that investors didn’t care or perhaps that the sum was smaller than they feared. As Jonathan Guilford pointed out, it’s a tiny amount relative to the roughly $80 billion of net income that analysts expect Meta to generate ​this year.
The legal payments are also spread
, opens new tab
 over a decade, which means they’re lower in today’s money than the headline figure suggests. For the sake of simplicity, assume 10 equal installments starting immediately and discounted at a 10% rate. The present value ​would be $12 billion, or 0.8% of Meta’s almost $1.5 trillion market capitalisation.
In India, meanwhile, Shritama Bose dug into a decision by the local regulator to bar a JPMorgan entity and another Mumbai-based broker. It’s part of a wider crackdown on what the watchdog sees as market manipulation in the country’s $6 trillion
, opens new tab
 equity derivatives market. The financial penalty in this case? Just a few hundred thousand dollars. That won’t trouble JPMorgan (JPM.N)
, opens new tab
 boss Jamie Dimon much.
True, in both cases the real punishment is arguably non-financial. Zuckerberg, for example, pledged meaningful changes to Meta’s apps, including age verification, limiting ​14-to-17-year-olds to two hours of usage and restricting night-time notifications. Yet Jonathan is sceptical that these tweaks will amount to much, concluding that Meta has ultimately paid a small price to secure its industry status.
More broadly, it’s notable that fines and ​other similar penalties don’t seem to have kept pace with soaring stock markets in recent years. Good Jobs First, a non-profit that “promotes corporate and government accountability in economic development”, keeps a database
, opens new tab
 that tracks regulatory punishments and other payouts related to corporate misconduct, including many ‌legal cases like ⁠those brought by state attorneys general.
Total annual U.S. penalties peaked at $84 billion in 2024, but that figure was not much bigger than the previous high of $81 billion in 2015. For comparison, the total value of the benchmark S&P 500 Index almost tripled over the same period. In other words, the drag to shareholders from corporate misconduct seems to be fading as a percentage of overall market capitalisation.
None of this is to say that Zuckerberg can rest easy. He will have a lot of other things on his mind this weekend. Robert Cyran, drawing on a Reuters investigation, on Wednesday examined why Meta’s efforts to remake itself around artificial intelligence have run into repeated setbacks.
The takeaway is striking. Technological revolutions are always tough for incumbents, and Meta ​is now one of them. That’s a far bigger problem ​for the company than a legal bill that failed ⁠to dent the share price.
Beijing has been tightening its grip on Chinese wealth held outside of the mainland, particularly in Hong Kong. It’s not great news for insurers like AIA and Prudential. Policies bought in the financial centre have long been a popular channel for mainland visitors to diversify their assets offshore. But as Katrina Hamlin showed in this chart on Thursday, which ​was published alongside a piece about Prudential’s results, the underlying demand is still strong. And some types of policies seem less vulnerable than others.
For a ​long time, the received wisdom among ⁠Western economists was that liberal democracy and capitalism go hand in hand. Today, that consensus lies in tatters. On The Big View
, opens new tab
, economist Daron Acemoglu tells Peter Thal Larsen that the institutions, laws and freedoms that made the West rich are under threat. The Nobel laureate has a plan to change that.
Over on the Viewsroom
, opens new tab
, Aimee Donnellan, Jonathan Guilford and Gabriel Rubin previewed Kevin Warsh’s first Jackson Hole symposium as chair of the Federal Reserve. His strategy of staying tight-lipped on interest rates, and hoping investors will focus on ⁠the real economy, ​may have long-term consequences.
Of all the so-called Trump trades
, opens new tab
 that rose to prominence at the start of the U.S. president’s second term, prison stocks ​have been arguably the most enduring. GEO (GEO.N)
, opens new tab
 and CoreCivic (CXW.N)
, opens new tab
 together oversee approximately 165 correctional facilities, with space for roughly 160,000 inmates. As Jeffrey Goldfarb writes, they’ve trounced the benchmark S&P 500 Index since November 2024, even though violent crime has been falling for years. An enlarged and emboldened Immigration and Customs ​Enforcement agency is keeping wardens busy, but it doesn’t look politically or financially sustainable.
